With Japan exporting lead pencils, matches, electric lamp bulbs, automobile tires, rubber boots, bathing suits, silk shirts, and stockings, along with a choice collection of rayon goods, toys, steel pipe, automobiles, bicycles, and even jackets for our "hot dogs," it behooves us to forget the open door in any other part of the world and to open the door to greater purchasing power at home.
That, Mr. Speaker, is exactly the contention I believe we all must be ready to support and take very seriously to heart. There are other extracts I should like to read, but I have not time to go into them all; they all point to the very rapid development of Japan and Russia in the export trade of the world, where they are coming into direct conflict with us.
The next point which I think we need to consider seriously is this: Is there any chance of recovering this trade? Let me read to you, Mr. Speaker, an extract from The Agricultural Situation and Outlook, published by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce in 1936. Let us mark these things very carefully and see what chance we have in this situation.
Agricultural protection in Europe has been increasing since 1925-
That was back in the days of the good old Liberal administration.
-and one of the characteristics of the depression has been the continuous narrowing of the free market open to exports of farm produce.

Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement
A summary of the increases in duties alone would be misleading as to the importance of restrictive measures, because the institution of quotas, milling regulations, import monopolies, licensing systems, and exchange controls operates even more effectively to cut off imports. The wide adoption of these barriers to trade was brought out by the Swedish publication Index, of February, 1935, in which it was shown that state trading monopolies were employed by two countries, import monopolies by seventeen, import licences by twenty-seven, import quotas by twenty-seven, export licences by thirteen, export quotas by sixteen, export subsidies by fourteen and exchange controls by thirty-six countries.
I submit that if the Liberal administration, or all of us working together, hope to solve the hopeless economic situation that exists in Canada to-day and put the unemployed to work by materially increasing our trade, against a situation like that, we have an optimism that is not justified.
Let me read something more, which is rather interesting as coming from the Secretary of the Treasury of the Roosevelt administration. I have always been impressed during the last two or three years by the fact that if there was anything to be gained in the way of export markets, the United States, having the great advantages that they have, and certainly being ready to go after any advantage that can be gained, would have obtained those markets. Now we find Mr. Morgenthau in a radio address on May 13, 1935, using the following words, which I submit should give us serious thought:
In estimating our foreign trade in relation to our monetary policy, we may as well face the question whether we wish to sell abroad vast quantities of goods that the buyers cannot pay for, unless we lend them the money.
Those few words contain a very large meaning. That is the conclusion that this man has come to after a trial of both the blasting policy and the other policy.
Hon. members may ask me: What is your solution? It is not my purpose to-night to state the solution. At present I am discussing this proposal that so many hon. members seem to think offers a solution. I maintain, as two hon. members from our group have already maintained, that this matter of tariffs is neither here nor there; it simply does not make any serious difference to the situation. It is all right for us to work for an increase of trade, but to delude ourselves into thinking that is the way to solve our problems is altogether unbecoming to intelligent men and women. Let me read an extract from an article in Harper's Monthly for January, 1936, called The Fallacy of Conquest, written by Nathaniel Peffer. It may be that this man does not
know what he is talking about, but he writes as though he does. He closes his article with this remarkable statement:
For a way out of the economic dilemma it is better to turn back into ourselves-
That is the stand of the Conservative party.
-reexamine our economic premises, and make the fundamental changes which are called for by the fact that the first epoch in the age of mechanization has irrevocably gone. The outlets must be found by reorganization at home, by making it possible for the disinherited at home to buy the goods we have hitherto counted on the heathen in the back woods to pay for.
At some later time I shall take the opportunity, if I am permitted, to say something about the sort of readjustment that, as I see it, should be made.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I
trust, Mr. Speaker, that my friend the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) will not consider it unbecoming or unintelligent on my part if I do not on this occasion attempt to deal with the argument which he has advanced. My time is limited, and rather than endeavour to deal with the question whether or not increase of trade offers a solution for our economic problems I shall confine myself to a consideration of the particular trade pact which is now before the house.
Prior to the introduction of the resolution to approve the Canada-United States trade pact, I had anticipated that the government would come forward with the proposed agreement, point out its benefits and advantages to Canada, and on that basis ask its adoption. But that course has not been pursued. Some private members supporting the government have outlined some of the particular sectional benefits which they hope will accrue to some electors whom they represent. The government itself as represented by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in their addresses have asked the adoption of this agreement on three grounds: First, that no one other than the Liberal party and the present Prime Minister could have made a trade agreement with the United States; second, that the former government through its Prime Minister offered to make an agreement in the same terms or practically the same terms, and therefore members of this party are estopped from opposing this agreement; and, third, that the government and those who support the trade agreement are actuated by pure motives and good intentions.
With respect to the first ground, that no one other than the present Prime Minister
Canada-UJS. Trade Agreement

and the Liberal party could have made a trade agreement with the United States, it seems to me that the history of trade agreements and trade negotiations with the United States, outlined by the Prime Minister and subsequently by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) clearly demonstrated how untenable is the statement of the Prime Minister to which I have referred. From long before I was born down to 1932 or 1933 the United States have been selling to Canada vast quantities and values of goods far in excess of what we were selling to them, resulting in heavy adverse trade balances annually. They were selling to. us manufactured or partly manufactured goods, and we in the main were selling to them raw or partly processed raw material. Despite that favourable trade balance to the United States, they in 1922 raised their tariffs against our comparatively small exports to that country. Why? I hope I do not give offence to our American neighbours when I answer my own question:	It was because the United States
have been the most aggressive exporting nation in the *world, while at the same time they have endeavoured to restrict imports as far as possible.
In the face of the Fordney-McCumber tariff of 1922 we did nothing. For eight long years we did nothing. Every time a proposal to increase tariffs against the United States came before the house the then government, led by the present Prime Minister, took the attitude that we in Canada should not retaliate. We were told, "Do not let us provoke Washington." Now I ask:	Why not
provoke Washington? The question was asked then, and I think I correctly interpret the answer which was given by that government through the present Prime Minister when I say that the answer was: Do not let us retaliate or provoke Washington, because if we do they may remove from their free list some of Canada's products which are now going into that country. This is just the same bogey as is offered us to-day as a reason why we should make the vast concessions that we are asked to make in the present trade agreement. Eight long years of non-provocative action did not result in any reductions in the United States tariff against us, nor any suggestions from that country that a trade agreement should be made between Canada and the United States.
In 1930, just before the election, the United States further increased their tariffs against Canada and raised further barriers against Canadian producers. In July of 1930 there was an election, and in August of that year

the Conservative party took office. In the fall a special session was called, and at that session some items in our general tariff were increased against all countries, including the United States. In the sessions of 1931 and 1932 there were further increases in our general tariff against all countries, including the United States. Was that provocative action? From the point of view of Liberals, they would say that it was provocative action. Did the United States then increase their tariff against us? They did not. Then, in 1932 the imperial trade agreements were negotiated by the Conservative government led by the present leader of the opposition.
The increases in our tariff of 1930, 1931 and 1932 impeded the flow of United States manufactured products into Canada, but the empire trade agreements made provision whereby part of that which United States interests had been exporting to Canada was supplied by the British empire. Then, and then only, for the first time was there talk from Washington about a trade agreement with Canada; then, and then only, for the first time did the American press carry reports suggesting that a trade agreement be made with Canada. This was caused, I submit, by pressure upon the Washington government from vast industrial interests in the United States whose export trade to this country was being transferred to the United Kingdom and other parts of the British empire. With that background to the picture I leave it to the judgment of this country as to whether the present Prime Minister or the present leader of the opposition, if both gentlemen were willing to make an agreement on practically the same basis, should be painted in the foreground as the person most likely to get a trade pact with the United States. I submit the statement that only the present Prime Minister could have concluded an agreement is but a vain boast.
I now turn to the allegation that the former government offered practically the same terms as those now embodied in the trade agreement, an allegation based upon a letter dated November 14, 1934, written by the Canadian Minister to the Secretary of State for the United States. To parts of that letter I shall refer, but as it has been read in the house I shall not repeat the whole of it. This letter, which has been called the basis of negotiations, suggested concessions which might be made mutually by each country, and then suggested further concessions in addition to those which were mutual which should be made by the United States.
Paragraph (c) stipulated a reduction by fifty per cent of the existing United States

Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement
rates of duty, as authorized by the Tariff Act of 1934, on a specified number of natural products, including, among other things, lumber, fish, potatoes, milk and cream, live cattle, a number of other agricultural products, and several minerals both metallic and non-metallic. One need only examine the schedules of the present agreement to see that there has not been a fifty per cent reduction in the items specified, much less those included in the general words of that section.
Turning to paragraph (d), in the basis for negotiations we find provision for a reduction of the existing rates of duty by the United States on a number of partly or wholly manufactured products of Canada- and I pause to emphasize the words "partly or wholly manufactured products of Canada'''-including some processed natural products and other items referred to therein. [DOT]
As I said, the agreement before us does not give a fifty per cent reduction as specified in paragraph (c), except in respect of some few items, and we have not received the reductions with respect to the partly manufactured or processed articles to which reference is made in paragraph (d). I should like to ask where in the basis of negotiations there was any suggestion that Canada should forego her right to fix fair market values under section 36, subsection 2, and section 43 of the Customs Act, or where there was any suggestion that we should be restricted in fixing the rate of discount under section 37. There was not a suggestion. It is true that in a letter of December 27, 1934, written by the Secretary of State of the United States to the Canadian Minister, the Secretary of State said:
I suggest that to the proposed outline of discussion-
Outline of discussion.
*-there be added the question of methods of determining the value of merchandise for duty purposes in either country, a matter which I consider of importance in the proposed negotiations.
But where, sir, I ask you, was there any such provision in the basis of negotiations, or where is there any record that the former Prime Minister would have agreed to or considered the concessions asked? Then, I ask: Where is there any provision in the basis of negotiations for concessions made by the present Prime Minister in the trade agreement containing a provision such as he has included in a letter written by the Canadian Legation to the Secretary of State for the United States, concurrently with the execution of this agreement, in which in clause (d) it is
agreed that in interpreting the words "of a class or kind made or produced in Canada" provision will be made to make it clear that the phrase "made or produced in Canada" in this context means "made or produced in Canada in commercial quantities." That letter does not clearly define what is meant by "made or produced in commercial quantities." But if we have reference to the notes exchanged between the government of Canada and that of Japan almost concurrently with the letter to which I have just referred we find there a definition, because in item 1 of the letter of December 26, 1935, we find the statement that "the classification 'goods of a class or kind made or produced in C anada, as it appears in the customs tariff, will be restricted to goods which are of a class or kind made or produced in Canada in quantities sufficient to supply at least ten per cent of the normal Canadian consumption." Find me in the basis of negotiations any suggestion of limiting our exports to the United States as to kind, such as the limitations in this trade agreement upon our exports of cod and haddock to the United States. It does seem to me that when as a necessary incident to the granting of the favoured nation treatment to the United States they obtained the benefit of direct shipment, thereby injuriously affecting our maritime ports, the government at least might have insisted upon some quid pro quo-although that expression is not liked by a lot of our Liberal friends-for those in the maritime provinces who were going to suffer.
Find me in the basis of negotiations any suggestions that Canada's exports to the United States should be limited to tiny percentages of the normal American consumption, such as the provision in this agreement with respect to cattle. If I were required to summarize the difference between this agreement and the proposals contained in the basis of negotiations of November 14, 1934. I would do so with one word-"Jobs"-" Jobs for our people in Canada." The basis of negotiations would have preserved the jobs of those now employed. The trade agreement as presented to the house will in my opinion-I hope to refer to this a little later-destroy some jobs which are now in existence. In my opinion the basis of negotiations would have created jobs

I come now to the third point: Pure motives and good intentions, as emphasized by my genial friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). The minister conceded, even to those of us who might oppose this agreement, pure motives and good intentions. I do likewise to all. I do not impute to the government that made this agreement a lack of good intentions, but at the same time I am ever mindful that it has been tritely said, "The road to hell is paved with good intentions." No trade agreement would be negotiated by the government of any country in the world if that government did not hope that it would bring some benefit to their country. In my opinion this agreement will unquestionably bring some benefit to Canada. I can readily appreciate that it may bring some immediate benefits to certain of the farmers of this country, but I do say that it will not bring any lasting benefits to the farmers because such benefits cannot be obtained from any mere trade agreement so long as the purchasing power of this dominion is so tremendously reduced by unemployment. There has been expressed in this house a thought which I think will bear repetition, that the finest market the Canadian mixed farmer will ever have is the hungry mouth of the urban and suburban worker, provided that he and his fellow workers have jobs and full pay envelopes. Unquestionably this agreement will bring some benefits, but in arriving at a conclusion as to its usefulness we must balance the detriments against the benefits. On balance, I, for one, find it wanting.
The two most important problems facing Canada, outside the field of pure finance, is finding markets for the disposition of our great surplus of wheat at a price which will bring something like a reasonable return to the growers, and finding jobs for our unemployed. When we realize that 82-9 per cent of our agricultural production is consumed in this country; when we realize that in 1929 Canada imported from the United States 68-6 per cent of all imports, imports which by far exceeded our exports to that country; when we realize that more than fifty per cent of our population to-day is not upon the farms but is in the cities and suburbs, it must be apparent to all that the primary purpose of any trade agreement which is to bring great benefit to this dominion should be not to make tariff reductions which

would cause more unemployment, but to try to get for our exports tariff reductions which would aid unemployment. I cannot see where this trade agreement fulfils that necessity. True, it may create some employment in the lumbering industry; true, it may create a few more jobs in the fishing industry, but where is there any provision in the agreement that is going to provide more jobs in the manufacturing industry of this country?
For example, consider our printing industry. A term of this trade agreement which was not even considered in the basis of negotiations is that the tax on advertising in magazines printed in the United States shall be repealed. Do we realize that the printing of American magazines in Canada because of that tax on advertising resulted in an expenditure of $800,000 in the printing industry and brought in through taxes a revenue of $600,000? Do we realize that of that $800,000 which was spent in the printing industry, $320,000 was paid in printer's wages? Do we realize that already 320 members of the printers' union in this country have lost their jobs? By no means have all the American magazines yet taken their printing back to the United States, but they are doing so. Is that providing more employment or losing it? Take the factories manufacturing radio cabinets and equipment for radio. They have let out their employees by hundreds; I am sorry I cannot give the figures. The Minister of Finance, when this question was raised, said: Oh, but the factories that are closing are American concerns with branch factories in this country. Well, Mr. Speaker, does it make one iota of difference whether it is a branch of an American concern or not so long as it is giving jobs to Canadian workers in Canadian factories?

Now I ask: Does anyone think that Canada as a whole can get any new industries so long as an industry in this country cannot secure the benefits of the special provisions of our tariff laws for goods of a class or kind made in Canada until their production equals ten per cent of Canadian consumption? How on earth will they ever get started under those conditions? I say to the house that the detriments of this trade agreement are not only that it fails on balance to create jobs, but I fear that it will cause a loss of jobs to many now employed, and therefore, because the detriments outweigh the advantages, I shall vote against the agreement.
Now that I have a moment or two left I want to refer to some of the statements that have been made by hon. members in this debate. More than one hon. member who has spoken in support of this agreement accused the Conservative party of following a doctrine of economic nationalism, and even when I enunciate that now, they applaud. They alleged that this trade agreement would be the end of economic nationalism. Well, economic nationalism, as I understand it, is a national opinion on the part of the people in any one country that they should preserve their own domestic market for any products that can be made in their own country, and at the same time unload their exports on other countries of the world. No one realizes better than I do. the fallacy of the doctrine of economic nationalism. But the difference between the doctrine of economic nationalism and that of sacrificing the interests of one's country in order to develop trade is a matter of degree. I do not favour economic nationalism,, but if opposing this trade agreement is economic nationalism, then, sir, I must stand convicted.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) introduced into this discussion a note to which I feel called upon to refer. He claimed that this trade agreement was the beginning of the end of economic imperialism. Economic imperialism, I suppose, I might define as a national opinion favourable to trading as far as possible within the British empire rather than with foreign countries. I believe that geographically the natural channels of trade and transportation on the north Ameri-12739-61
can continent are north and south. I came to a realization of that fact many, many years ago, but at the same time I concluded that the national cost of directing a large proportion of that trade and transportation east and west was part of the price we pay for the privilege, for the many privileges, of being part and parcel of the British empire. I for one am willing to continue to pay that price. Now, do not misunderstand me. I do not say that this trade agreement will give the United States economic domination in this country, but when I see that during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929, we purchased 68-6 per cent of all our imports from the United States, in 1930, 67-9 per cent, in 1931, 61-5 per cent, and so on, the percentage decreasing each year, and then when I see this trade agreement which is bound to increase again the imports of this country from the United States, I say that this trade agreement is making a serious contribution to the economic domination of this country by the United States.
I want to make a further statement, one that is frequently laughed at, but one which I think must be regarded in all seriousness. If this country ever comes under the economic domination of the United States it will be a question of only a very short time until we are one or more of the states of the American union.

Mr. Speaker, the house has been discussing the motion before it for nearly a fortnight, almost to the exclusion of everything else. In that course of time the subject matter of the resolution has been very thoroughly debated. It would be but occupying unnecessarily the time of hon. members to go over the ground that already has been traversed so well by other speakers. About all I wish to say at the moment is that, having regard to the importance of this agreement, it can truthfully be said that there has never been introduced before in the Commons of Canada an agreement of such great importance which has been so generally approved and so ineffectively criticized as the present one. The force of this observation is all the greater in view of the fact that this is the first session of a new parliament comprising in its membership groups not hitherto represented in this house.
The approval has been all but unanimous, if we except what is left of the old Conservative party in the house at the present time. I believe, with this exception, it might be said to be unanimous. I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that the house is overwhelmingly Liberal, and that with respect to this agreement there has not been a dissenting voice so far as the Liberal party is concerned. That is the more remarkable when it is recalled that the Liberal following is drawn from constituencies of all kinds, rural and urban, and from all parts of Canada. There are members here of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party who were in the house during previous parliaments; they have in their ranks some new members. They, too, old and new alike, so far as they have spoken, have spoken favourably and approvingly of the agreement. There is another party which has come in with a considerable membership, the Social Credit party. In so far as its members have spoken their words also have been not of criticism but of approval of the agreement. There remains yet one other party, the Social Reconstruction party. It, too, has been unanimous in its commendation of the agreement. All that is left in opposition to the agreement is the remnant of the Tory party

in the house at the present time. After listening to the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite who belong to that party, one thing, I think, is clear, namely, that no agreement with the United States would ever have been concluded by that party, under any circumstances whatever. Their argument, from that of the leader himself (Mr. Bennett) and throughout its ranks, has been that an agreement with the United States meant trade north and south, meant the end of the building up of Canada, meant the breaking up of the British empire, meant annexation, meant getting away from the British flag, and all that sort of thing to which the country has listened from Tory speakers for half a century past. That has been the sole contribution of hon. gentlemen opposite to the discussion of this great measure. I do not purpose, therefore, to spend any time in commenting on the line of attack they have made.
One misconception, however, which I should like to point out is that stressed by the last speaker who addressed the house (Mr. Lawson) as he kept making comparisons between what was set forth as the basis of negotiation of an agreement and the present agreement, as if the basis of negotiation of the agreement had been the agreement that hon. gentlemen opposite would have secured or ever thought they were going to get. His own leader made it quite clear that there is a distinction to be drawn between the basis of negotiation of an agreement and an agreement itself. As has been so well pointed out by other speakers, it is not usual for parties negotiating an agreement to make the basis of an agreement less than or equal to what they expect ultimately to receive. In fact, they usually seek to have the basis of agreement cover demands far beyond anything they ever expect actually to receive. The comparisons of the hon. member for South York are all beside the question.
I do take exception, very strong exception, Mr. Speaker, to the right hon. the leader of the opposition saying that he could or might have secured an agreement, to all intents and purposes, very similar to or substantially the same as the one which has been obtained by the present government. I think my right hon. friend knows that that is not correct. He knows of course, as an old parliamentarian and as one who has had much to do with the conduct of international affairs, that we are both precluded from telling the house the actual state of negotiations under his administration and what followed when the new administration came into office. To that extent certainly I am very much handicapped in trying to review what my hon. friend has-

I have in my hand a copy of an article which appeared in the Mail and Empire of November 5. It is headed: Acid test for King. Ability to secure mutually satisfactory agreement challenged. It begins:

Had anything of that kind existed in this agreement, it would have materially affected the whole agreement from the point of view of the benefit to be derived from its provisions by the cattle industry. So I say, Mr. Speaker, that just taking what appears to be a more or less accurate statement of the situation, which I should say was probably inspired, there is ample evidence that the agreement as it is before the house for approval goes very much further in the interests of Canada than anything my right hon. friend found it possible to obtain prior to the time he went out of office.
I might mention other features. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Stewart) took a characteristic line, when indicating what he termed the many concessions the United States got compared with what Canada secured. He started off with oranges. I think this is as good an illustration as could be used; he said:
Let us see what Canada gives, as compared with what she gets. She gives concessions on oranges to the value of $21,000,000-
First, as to the meaning and accuracy of the figures used, what does my hon. friend mean when he says that the United States got concessions to the extent of $21,000,000 on oranges? I do not know where he obtained his figures; I am told that according to our own statistical department the duty collected on oranges since they were placed on the dutiable list by the late administration, that is for the four years combined, was less than $5,000,000, and that the value of imports of oranges from all countries in the peak year, 1929, was only $9,500,000, while the com-

bined imports of the last four years totalled less than $21,000,000. Yet my hon. friend from
Leeds says, "Look at the concession the United States got, $21,000,000 on oranges."
What I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, is this: In discussing this agreement hon. gentlemen opposite seem to have considered only the alleged interests of producers, even where, as in the case of oranges, there are no producers in Canada. They have not had one word to say for the poor consumer, all the way through. Yet so far as Canada is concerned every one is a consumer, and there is not a producer who does not also receive something from any benefit obtained by consumers. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat says, "Where is the help for the manufacturers in this agreement?" Well, if the consumers are going to derive the great benefit hon. gentlemen opposite would seem to imagine through the intermediate tariff being granted to the United States, that is going to be of assistance to every manufacturer in the country because it will increase the real wages of the workingmen of Canada, and whatever will help the manufacturers or producers lessen the cost of production and the cost of living is going to be of material help to the manufacturers and producers themselves. There is in addition the demand for manufactured goods which will come from the purchasing power derived from the sale of Canada's primary and other products in the United States. But for each single producer in the country it is difficult to say just how many consumers there are; we are all consumers, and the difference between hon. gentlemen opposite and ourselves is that we have been looking to the well-being of the consumers as well as to that of the producers. They have been confining their attention almost exclusively to what is going to benefit certain special or vested interests in the country.
I need not enlarge upon the benefits afforded by the agreement to consumers; the benefits run all through the agreement, but may I say that what might have been a substantial benefit to consumers five years ago through giving to the United States or other countries the intermediate tariff is very much less of a benefit to-day. In many particulars the intermediate tariff to-day is almost the same as the general tariff. During the time my right hon. friend was in office he hardly let a session go by, in fact, I do not think he did let a session go by, without jacking up the tariff somewhat higher, and in particular bringing the intermediate tariff nearer to the level of the general tariff. As a result, when to-day we speak of giving another country the bene-

Canada~U.S. Trade Agreement
fits of the intermediate tariff actually we are giving it a tariff which to all intents and purposes is considerably higher than the general tariff was when the Liberal party was in office. In regard to this agreement let me repeat that as far as we are concerned one of its chief benefits is what we hope and believe it will do for the consumers of Canada. In helping the consumers we believe it is going to help all classes, and every family and household.
My hon. friend from Leeds also touched on a point that I do not think was mentioned by anyone else; just how he came to see it I do not know. My hon. friend spoke about the three escape clauses; he pointed out that there were in this agreement three clauses whereby its term could be shortened so that it might not run for the full three years. If someone from this side of the house had presented that argument with a view to having the condition remedied, there might have been something to it, but my hon. friend was arguing all the time that the agreement was a bad one, and I think in the circumstances he should have been happy that there were some clauses in it which would enable its term to be shortened if necessary.
